Briefly explaining the meaning: This section briefly explains the meaning of the preceding verse. It is divided into two parts: first, the general explanation; second, the specific explanation. First, the general explanation: Although there are many types of afflictions, they are subsumed under the three poisons. Furthermore, because these three poisons encompass all afflictions, they are explained in detail. Second, the specific explanation: This section specifically explains the meaning of the preceding verse. It is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the three poisons; second, the explanation of the three sufferings. First, the explanation of the three poisons: This section explains the three poisons in detail. It is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of ignorance; second, the explanation of craving; third, the explanation of hatred. First, the explanation of ignorance: Ignorance is the root of all afflictions. Because it is the most fundamental, it is explained first. Second, the explanation of craving: Craving is the cause of birth and death. Because it binds one to the cycle of existence, it is explained next. Third, the explanation of hatred: Hatred obstructs the path to liberation. Because it causes harm to oneself and others, it is explained last. Second, the explanation of the three sufferings: This section explains the three sufferings in detail. It is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the suffering of birth; second, the explanation of the suffering of aging; third, the explanation of the suffering of death. First, the explanation of the suffering of birth: Birth involves the pain of emerging from the womb and the exhaustion of the physical form. Second, the explanation of the suffering of aging: Aging involves the decline of the faculties and the loss of vitality. Third, the explanation of the suffering of death: Death involves the separation from loved ones and the dissolution of the body. (End of Part II) III. Resolving the obstacles (divided into two): 1. Resolving the objection regarding the inclusion of the three poisons within the three sufferings; 2. Resolving the objection regarding the sequence of the three poisons. 1. Resolving the objection regarding the inclusion of the three poisons within the three sufferings: Some may object that since the three poisons are already included within the three sufferings, they should not be explained separately. This is resolved by noting that while the three poisons are indeed subsumed under the three sufferings, their distinct natures and functions require separate explanation for the sake of clarity. 2. Resolving the objection regarding the sequence of the three poisons: Some may object that the sequence of the three poisons—ignorance, craving, and hatred—is not fixed. This is resolved by noting that this sequence follows the order of their arising in the process of dependent origination and their relative gravity in terms of obstruction to liberation. Just as a mani jewel, when placed near various colors, appears to take on those colors, yet possesses no inherent color of its own; so too does the body of the Tathāgata, through the power of his original vows, appear in various forms according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings. It is not that the Buddha-body undergoes transformation, but rather that it manifests in accordance with the mental dispositions of those to be trained. This is called the "Parable of the Mani Jewel. Regarding the first, the five types of ignorance: first, ignorance regarding the past; second, ignorance regarding the future; third, ignorance regarding both the past and the future; fourth, ignorance regarding the principle of dependent origination; and fifth, ignorance regarding the noble truths. Among these, the first three constitute the error of being confused about phenomena and their meaning. As for the first, ignorance regarding the past: it refers to the lack of knowledge concerning the prior limit of existence—that is, the state of sentient beings in previous lives—due to the obscuration of the afflictions. As for the second, ignorance regarding the future: it refers to the lack of knowledge concerning the subsequent limit of existence—that is, the state of sentient beings in future lives—due to the obscuration of the afflictions. As for the third, ignorance regarding both the past and the future: it refers to the lack of knowledge concerning the intermediate state between those two limits—that is, the present life—due to the obscuration of the afflictions. Because one is thus ignorant of the three periods of time, one fails to understand that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Furthermore, because one is ignorant of the causes and effects of the three periods of time, one does not know that the various realms of existence arise from the power of karma and afflictions, nor does one know that the various states of rebirth arise from the power of karma and afflictions. Moreover, because one is ignorant of the three periods of time, one does not know that the cessation of the three periods of time arises from the power of the path, nor does one know that the cessation of the various realms of existence arises from the power of the path. Consequently, one cannot generate the mind of renunciation toward saṃsāra, nor can one generate the mind of seeking liberation toward nirvāṇa. This is called the error of being confused about phenomena and their meaning. As for the fourth, ignorance regarding the principle of dependent origination: it refers to the lack of knowledge concerning the twelve links of dependent origination due to the obscuration of the afflictions. Because one is ignorant of the twelve links of dependent origination, one does not know that the various realms of existence arise from the power of karma and afflictions, nor does one know that the various states of rebirth arise from the power of karma and afflictions. Furthermore, because one is ignorant of the twelve links of dependent origination, one does not know that the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination arises from the power of the path, nor does one know that the cessation of the various realms of existence arises from the power of the path. Consequently, one cannot generate the mind of renunciation toward saṃsāra, nor can one generate the mind of seeking liberation toward nirvāṇa. This is called the error of being confused about phenomena and their meaning. As for the fifth, ignorance regarding the noble truths: it refers to the lack of knowledge concerning the four noble truths due to the obscuration of the afflictions. Because one is ignorant of the four noble truths, one does not know that the various realms of existence arise from the power of karma and afflictions, nor does one know that the various states of rebirth arise from the power of karma and afflictions. Furthermore, because one is ignorant of the four noble truths, one does not know that the cessation of the four noble truths arises from the power of the path, nor does one know that the cessation of the various realms of existence arises from the power of the path. Consequently, one cannot generate the mind of renunciation toward saṃsāra, nor can one generate the mind of seeking liberation toward nirvāṇa. This is called the error of being confused about phenomena and their meaning. Regarding the second part, the two errors concerning the confusion of persons and their meaning: first, ignorance regarding the self; and second, ignorance regarding the sentient beings. Among these, the first, ignorance regarding the self: it refers to the lack of knowledge concerning the self due to the obscuration of the afflictions. Because one is ignorant of the self, one does not know that the various realms of existence arise from the power of karma and afflictions, nor does one know that the various states of rebirth arise from the power of karma and afflictions. Furthermore, because one is ignorant of the self, one does not know that the cessation of the self arises from the power of the path, nor does one know that the cessation of the various realms of existence arises from the power of the path. Consequently, one cannot generate the mind of renunciation toward saṃsāra, nor can one generate the mind of seeking liberation toward nirvāṇa. This is called the error of being confused about persons and their meaning. As for the second, ignorance regarding the sentient beings: it refers to the lack of knowledge concerning sentient beings due to the obscuration of the afflictions. Because one is ignorant of sentient beings, one does not know that the various realms of existence arise from the power of karma and afflictions, nor does one know that the various states of rebirth arise from the power of karma and afflictions. Furthermore, because one is ignorant of sentient beings, one does not know that the cessation of sentient beings arises from the power of the path, nor does one know that the cessation of the various realms of existence arises from the power of the path. Consequently, one cannot generate the mind of renunciation toward saṃsāra, nor can one generate the mind of seeking liberation toward nirvāṇa. This is called the error of being confused about persons and their meaning. These are collectively termed the five types of ignorance. Initial Announcement and Permission to Speak At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly: "O monks, listen attentively and bear well in mind what I shall now expound. Having spoken thus, he granted permission for the discourse. II. Proper Exposition of the Characteristics This section consists of two parts: first, the general introduction; second, the detailed exposition. A. General Introduction The Buddha addressed the assembly: "O monks, there are three kinds of persons who, having heard this Dharma-gate, will not give rise to fear, doubt, or hesitation. B. Detailed Exposition This section consists of three parts: first, the enumeration of the names; second, the explanation of the characteristics; third, the conclusion regarding the benefits. 1. Enumeration of the Names What are the three? First, the person of dull faculties; second, the person of medium faculties; third, the person of sharp faculties. 2. Explanation of the Characteristics First, the person of dull faculties: although they hear this teaching, their roots of wisdom are weak and their afflictions are heavy, so they are unable to enter into deep contemplation. Second, the person of medium faculties: their roots of wisdom are moderate and their afflictions are neither too heavy nor too light; they can enter into contemplation with some effort. Third, the person of sharp faculties: their roots of wisdom are keen and their afflictions are light; they can immediately enter into profound contemplation upon hearing the teaching. 3. Conclusion Regarding the Benefits If these three types of persons practice as instructed, they will gradually sever the bonds of birth and death and attain the fruit of Arhatship, never again falling back into the cycle of existence. Thus, this Dharma-gate is of great benefit and should be widely propagated. III. Initial Sectional Analysis This section consists of three parts: first, the analysis of the subject matter; second, the analysis of the structure; third, the analysis of the sequence. A. Analysis of the Subject Matter The subject matter herein concerns the distinctions among the capacities of sentient beings and the methods for guiding them toward liberation. B. Analysis of the Structure The text is divided into three major sections: the introduction, the main body, and the conclusion. Each section further contains specific sub-divisions. C. Analysis of the Sequence The sequence follows a logical progression: first, the announcement of the teaching; second, the exposition of the characteristics; third, the summary of the benefits. This order ensures that the listener first gains confidence in the discourse, then understands its content, and finally realizes its practical value.
